notes:
Basic Terms

  • Objective function: the linear function of the decision variables to be maximised or minimised, e.g. $Z=ax+by$.
  • Constraints: linear inequalities/equations restricting the variables; together with $x\ge0,\ y\ge0$ (non-negative restrictions) they define the feasible region — the common region satisfying all constraints.
  • A point in the feasible region is a feasible solution; the point(s) that optimise $Z$ give the optimal solution.

Corner Point Method

  • The feasible region of an LPP is always a convex region (a convex polygon if bounded).
  • Corner Point Theorem: if the feasible region is bounded, the objective function attains both its maximum and minimum at corner points (vertices) of the feasible region.
  • Steps: (1) sketch the feasible region and find its corner points by solving pairs of boundary equations; (2) evaluate $Z$ at every corner point; (3) the largest/smallest value is the maximum/minimum.
  • If the feasible region is unbounded, a maximum or minimum may or may not exist; it must be verified by checking whether the half-plane $ax+by>M$ (or $
  • If two corner points give the same optimal $Z$ and the edge joining them lies on the boundary, then every point of that edge is also optimal — infinitely many optimal solutions. If the constraints admit no common point in the first quadrant, the LPP has no feasible solution.

Types of LPP

  • Manufacturing (maximise profit/output given machine-hours), diet (minimise cost given nutrient requirements), transportation (minimise cost given supply/demand) — all are modelled the same way: define decision variables, write the objective function, then translate each resource limit into a linear inequality.

Exam tip

KCET usually asks 2–3 questions from this chapter, almost always of the form: identify the corner points of a given feasible region and pick the maximum/minimum of $Z$. Sketch quickly, mark every boundary intersection lying in the first quadrant, and evaluate $Z$ at each — do not try to guess the answer from slopes under time pressure.

questions.q: In a linear programming problem, the common region determined by all the constraints (including $x\ge0,y\ge0$) is called the
questions.explanation: By definition, the set of all points satisfying every constraint simultaneously is called the feasible region.

questions.q: According to the Corner Point Theorem, if the feasible region of an LPP is bounded, the objective function attains its maximum and minimum at
options: the centroid of the feasible region
corner points of the feasible region
questions.explanation: The Corner Point Theorem states that for a bounded feasible region, the optimal values of a linear objective function occur at corner points (vertices).

questions.q: A point that satisfies all the constraints of a linear programming problem, including the non-negativity restrictions, is called a
questions.explanation: Any point lying in the feasible region is, by definition, a feasible solution.

questions.q: Maximise $Z = 3x + 4y$ subject to $x+y\le4$, $x\ge0$, $y\ge0$. The maximum value of $Z$ is
questions.explanation: Corner points are $(0,0), (4,0), (0,4)$ with $Z = 0, 12, 16$ respectively; the maximum is $16$.

questions.q: Maximise $Z = 3x + 4y$ subject to $x+y\le4$, $x,y\ge0$. The maximum occurs at the corner point
questions.explanation: $Z(0,4) = 16$ is the largest of the three corner values $0, 12, 16$.

questions.q: Minimise $Z = 200x + 500y$ subject to $x+2y\ge10$, $3x+4y\le24$, $x,y\ge0$. The minimum value of $Z$ is
questions.explanation: The feasible corner points are $(0,5), (0,6), (4,3)$ with $Z = 2500, 3000, 2300$; the minimum is $2300$.

questions.q: Minimise $Z = 200x + 500y$ subject to $x+2y\ge10$, $3x+4y\le24$, $x,y\ge0$. The minimum value of $Z$ occurs at the corner point
questions.explanation: $(4,3)$ is the intersection of $x+2y=10$ and $3x+4y=24$, and gives $Z=200(4)+500(3)=2300$, the smallest of the corner values.

questions.q: "If the feasible region of an LPP is unbounded, a maximum or a minimum of the objective function may fail to exist." This statement is
questions.explanation: For an unbounded feasible region, an optimal value (max or min) exists only if the corresponding half-plane test confirms it; otherwise it may not exist, so the statement is true in general.

questions.q: Maximise $Z = x + y$ subject to $x+y\le10$, $x\le6$, $y\le6$, $x,y\ge0$. This problem has
questions.explanation: Since $Z=x+y$ is parallel to the constraint line $x+y=10$, every point on the edge from $(6,4)$ to $(4,6)$ gives the same maximum value, so there are infinitely many optimal solutions.

questions.q: Maximise $Z = x + y$ subject to $x+y\le10$, $x\le6$, $y\le6$, $x,y\ge0$. The maximum value of $Z$ is
questions.explanation: At any point on the boundary edge $x+y=10$ within the feasible region, $Z=x+y=10$, which is the maximum.

questions.q: The feasible region of a linear programming problem is always a
questions.explanation: Since it is the intersection of half-planes, the feasible region of an LPP is always convex.

questions.q: Maximise $Z = 5x + 3y$ subject to $3x+5y\le15$, $5x+2y\le10$, $x,y\ge0$. The maximum value of $Z$ is
questions.explanation: Corner points are $(0,0), (2,0), \left(\dfrac{20}{19},\dfrac{45}{19}\right), (0,3)$ giving $Z = 0, 10, \dfrac{235}{19}\approx12.4, 9$; the maximum is $\dfrac{235}{19}$.

questions.q: Maximise $Z = 5x + 3y$ subject to $3x+5y\le15$, $5x+2y\le10$, $x,y\ge0$. The maximum of $Z$ occurs at the corner point
questions.explanation: Solving $3x+5y=15$ and $5x+2y=10$ simultaneously gives $x=20/19, y=45/19$, which yields the highest $Z$ value among all corners.

questions.q: The linear function of the variables which is to be maximised or minimised in an LPP is called the
questions.explanation: By definition, this is called the objective function, usually written $Z = ax+by$.

questions.q: The conditions $x\ge0, y\ge0$ in a linear programming problem are called the
questions.explanation: These conditions, required because decision variables usually represent quantities, are called non-negative restrictions.

questions.q: Consider minimising $Z=3x+2y$ subject to $x+y\ge8$, $3x+5y\le15$, $x,y\ge0$. This LPP has
questions.explanation: Along $x+y=8$ in the first quadrant, $3x+5y$ ranges from $24$ (at $(8,0)$) upward, always exceeding $15$; hence no point satisfies both constraints, so there is no feasible region.

questions.q: A firm makes chairs ($x$) and tables ($y$). Each chair needs 2 h of carpentry and 1 h of finishing; each table needs 1 h of carpentry and 2 h of finishing. Carpentry time available is 60 h and finishing time is 48 h per week. The correct constraints (besides $x,y\ge0$) are
questions.explanation: Total carpentry time used is $2x+y$, capped at 60 h; total finishing time used is $x+2y$, capped at 48 h.

questions.q: Maximise $Z=4x+y$ subject to $x+y\le50$, $3x+y\le90$, $x,y\ge0$. The maximum value of $Z$ is
Which of the following is NOT a requirement of a (standard) linear programming problem?
options: the decision variables must be integers
the constraints must be linear inequalities or equations
the decision variables must be non-negative
the objective function must be linear in the decision variables
questions.explanation: Standard LPPs allow continuous (real-valued) decision variables; requiring integer values defines the separate topic of integer programming.

questions.q: A feasible solution that maximises or minimises the objective function of an LPP is called the
questions.explanation: By definition, the feasible solution that gives the best (maximum or minimum) value of $Z$ is called the optimal solution.

questions.q: The graphical method of solving a linear programming problem can be directly applied only when the number of decision variables is at most
questions.explanation: A 2-D graph can represent at most two decision variables, so the graphical method is limited to LPPs with two decision variables.

questions.q: Maximise $Z=x+2y$ subject to $x+y\le6$, $x,y\ge0$. The maximum value of $Z$ is
questions.explanation: Corner points are $(0,0),(6,0),(0,6)$ with $Z=0,6,12$; the maximum is $12$.

questions.q: Maximise $Z=x+2y$ subject to $x+y\le6$, $x,y\ge0$. The maximum of $Z$ occurs at the corner point
questions.explanation: $Z(0,6)=12$ is the largest among the corner values $0,6,12$.

questions.q: Minimise $Z=2x+3y$ subject to $x+y\ge6$, $x,y\ge0$. The minimum value of $Z$ is
questions.explanation: The relevant corner points are $(6,0)$ and $(0,6)$ with $Z=12,18$; since $Z$ only increases moving away from $(6,0)$, the minimum is $12$.

questions.q: For the constraints $x+y\le10$, $x\ge0$, $y\ge0$, the point $(2,3)$ is
questions.explanation: Since $2+3=5\le10$ and both coordinates are non-negative, $(2,3)$ satisfies all constraints, so it is a feasible solution (though not a corner point).

questions.q: The feasible region defined by $x\ge0$, $y\ge0$, $x+y\le5$ has how many corner points?
questions.explanation: The region is a triangle with vertices $(0,0),(5,0),(0,5)$, giving 3 corner points.

questions.q: Maximise $Z=50x+40y$ subject to $2x+y\le12$, $x+2y\le14$, $x,y\ge0$. The maximum value of $Z$ is
questions.explanation: Corner points are $(0,0),(6,0),\left(\dfrac{10}{3},\dfrac{16}{3}\right),(0,7)$ with $Z=0,300,380,280$; the maximum is $380$.

questions.q: Maximise $Z=50x+40y$ subject to $2x+y\le12$, $x+2y\le14$, $x,y\ge0$. The maximum of $Z$ occurs at the corner point
questions.explanation: Solving $2x+y=12$ and $x+2y=14$ together gives $x=10/3,y=16/3$, which yields the highest $Z$ value among the corners.

questions.q: Minimise $Z=200x+300y$ subject to $x+2y\ge10$, $3x+4y\ge24$, $x,y\ge0$. The minimum value of $Z$ is
questions.explanation: The corner points are $(0,6),(4,3),(10,0)$ with $Z=1800,1700,2000$; the minimum is $1700$ at $(4,3)$.

questions.q: If the only constraints on an LPP are $x\ge0$ and $y\ge0$ (no other restriction), the feasible region is
questions.explanation: With no upper bound on $x$ or $y$, every point in the first quadrant satisfies both constraints, so the feasible region is the whole (unbounded) first quadrant.

questions.q: For a maximisation LPP with an unbounded feasible region, if the open half-plane $ax+by>M$ has no point in common with the feasible region (where $M$ is the value of $Z$ at some corner point), then the LPP
options: definitely has a maximum value, attained at that corner point
questions.explanation: This is exactly the test used to confirm that a maximum exists on an unbounded region: it exists and equals $M$, attained at the corresponding corner point.

questions.q: Maximise $Z=3x+5y$ subject to $x+y\le2$, $3x+y\le3$, $x,y\ge0$. The maximum value of $Z$ is
questions.explanation: Corner points are $(0,0),(1,0),(0.5,1.5),(0,2)$ with $Z=0,3,9,10$; the maximum is $10$.

questions.q: Maximise $Z=3x+5y$ subject to $x+y\le2$, $3x+y\le3$, $x,y\ge0$. The maximum of $Z$ occurs at the corner point
questions.explanation: $Z(0,2)=10$ is the largest of the corner values $0,3,9,10$.

questions.q: Minimise $Z=3x+2y$ subject to $x+y\ge6$, $2x+y\ge10$, $x,y\ge0$. The minimum value of $Z$ is
questions.explanation: Corner points are $(0,10),(4,2),(6,0)$ with $Z=20,16,18$; the minimum is $16$.

questions.q: Minimise $Z=3x+2y$ subject to $x+y\ge6$, $2x+y\ge10$, $x,y\ge0$. The minimum occurs at the corner point
questions.explanation: $Z(4,2)=16$ is the smallest of the corner values $20,18,16$, and $(4,2)$ is where the two boundary lines cross.

questions.q: A constraint that does not change the feasible region at all (every point satisfying the other constraints automatically satisfies it) is called
questions.explanation: Such a constraint adds no new restriction and is therefore called redundant.

questions.q: A diet must supply at least 10 units of a nutrient from foods X and Y, with $2x+y\ge10$ and $x+3y\ge15$ (x,y = units of X,Y), $x,y\ge0$. If food X costs Rs 4/unit and Y costs Rs 3/unit, the minimum cost is
questions.explanation: Minimise $Z=4x+3y$; corner points are $(0,10),(3,4),(15,0)$ with $Z=30,24,60$. The minimum cost is Rs 24, using 3 units of X and 4 of Y.

questions.q: Maximise $Z=5x+3y$ subject to $x+2y\le10$, $3x+y\le15$, $x,y\ge0$. The maximum value of $Z$ is
questions.explanation: Corner points are $(0,0),(5,0),(4,3),(0,5)$ with $Z=0,25,29,15$; the maximum is $29$ at $(4,3)$.

questions.q: A firm makes products X and Y; each unit of X needs 3 h on machine A and 1 h on machine B, each unit of Y needs 1 h on A and 2 h on B. Machine A has 12 h and machine B has 8 h available. Profit is Rs 6 per unit of X and Rs 4 per unit of Y. The maximum possible profit is
questions.explanation: Maximise $Z=6x+4y$ subject to $3x+y\le12$, $x+2y\le8$; corner points give $Z=0,24,16$ and, at $\left(\dfrac{16}{5},\dfrac{12}{5}\right)$, $Z=\dfrac{144}{5}=28.8$, the maximum.

questions.q: For the LPP: maximise $Z=x+y$ subject to $x-y\le1$, $x+y\ge2$, $x,y\ge0$, the objective function
questions.explanation: The feasible region extends without bound along $x-y=1$ as $x,y\to\infty$ (e.g. points $(t,t-1)$ for large $t$), so $Z=x+y$ increases without bound and has no maximum.
